Write a natural short email exchange. Subject: Dinner. Participants: Me, Ben; Me is the owner's speaker label, not a spoken name. Date: 2026-10-14, local time 10:15–11:45.
Earlier messages in this same thread, with their dates (context, not text to repeat):
2026-10-12 Ben: Hi! Following up from our DM — here's the address for dinner Thursday at 7pm at Juniper Cafe:

45 Elm Street. See you there!
2026-10-12 Me: Thanks Ben! Confirming our same plan from DM — Thursday at 7pm at Juniper Cafe.

See you then!
2026-10-13 Ben: Hi! Writing from work — bad news on my end.

A work deadline just came up and I can't get away Thursday evening. Can we move our dinner to Saturday at 7pm instead? Still Juniper Cafe?

Let me know if that works!

On Oct 12, Ben wrote:
> Hi! Following up from our DM — here's the address for dinner Thursday at 7pm at Juniper Cafe:
>
> 45 Elm Street. See you there!
2026-10-13 Me: No worries at all, work happens!

Saturday at 7pm at Juniper Cafe works for me. Let's do Saturday instead of Thursday. See you then!
Continue naturally. People remember the prior exchange and do not recap settled details unless conversation calls for it. Respect any gap between those dates and today's date; don't reply as if an old message just arrived.

Scenario: Ben replies that the restaurant has the revised booking. Include a normal nested reply chain below the new body: the previous reschedule email and its older quoted Thursday confirmation. Do not present quoted old details as a new proposal.

The conversation must naturally and unambiguously establish each of these facts (they are authoring constraints, not lines to copy):
1. The one current dinner with Ben is still Saturday at 7 pm at Juniper Cafe. Quoted Thursday details remain history, not a second booking.
Use 2–6 short emails. The subject is header metadata; do not put a Subject: prefix inside an email body. Return only JSON with dialogue (an array of {"sender": "Name", "body": "email text"}) and writer_note (a short string). Bodies may contain paragraphs and quoted replies using escaped newlines.
